summary: In Greek mythology, Brontes is one of the three elder Cyclopes, a brother of Arges and Steropes. The sons of Uranus and Gaia, these one-eyed giants were the brothers of the Titans and the master craftsmen of the gods. Their names, meaning "Thunder," "Bright," and "Lightning," reflect their defining role as the makers of Zeus's thunderbolt. Imprisoned beneath the earth, the brothers were freed and rewarded the gods with the divine weapons that decided the succession in heaven.
etymology: From the Greek Brontes (Βρόντης), meaning "Thunder" (brontē). The names Hesiod gives the three Cyclopes — Arges ("Bright"), Brontes ("Thunder"), and Steropes ("Lightning") — together describe the components of the thunderbolt they forge.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: Brontes belongs to the group known as the elder or Hesiodic Cyclopes, alongside his brothers Steropes and Arges. In Hesiod's Theogony, Gaia (Earth) bears the Cyclopes to Uranus (Sky), making them brothers of the Titans and members of the first generation of cosmic powers.

The three are described as having very violent hearts and a single round eye set in the middle of the forehead. They are distinct from the savage one-eyed shepherds, such as Polyphemus, who appear in later traditions like Homer's Odyssey.

sections.heading: Role and Mythology
paragraphs: Brontes and his brothers are the smiths of the gods, and their defining act is the forging of Zeus's all-powerful thunderbolt. This weapon plays a central part in the Greek succession myth, helping Zeus secure rule over the cosmos.

The brothers were first imprisoned by their father Uranus and confined beneath the earth. Zeus later freed the Cyclopes, and in return they gave him the thunderbolt — the gift that armed him for his victory in the struggle for divine kingship.

sections.heading: Death and Later Depictions
paragraphs: Some later accounts tell that Apollo killed the Cyclopes in revenge after Zeus struck down his son Asclepius with a thunderbolt of their making; in variant versions Apollo slays not the Cyclopes themselves but their sons.
Roman poetry continued to portray the brothers at work. In Virgil's Aeneid, Brontes labors with Steropes in the forge of Vulcan beneath Mount Etna, hammering out weapons and armor for the gods.
